Design-based Causal Inference

Defining causal effects

  • (Splawa-Neyman, Dabrowska, and Speed 1990), (Rubin 1974, 1978), (Holland 1986): A causal effect can be defined as a contrast between “potential outcomes.”
  • That is, for every observed (factual) outcome, there is an unobserved (counterfactual) outcome.
  • We begin, therefore, with meta-physics (Inwagen, Sullivan, and Bernstein 2023).
    • One (negative) definition by way of the logical positivists:

    The meaning of a statement consists entirely in the predictions it makes about possible experience

The Science

Population \(\mathcal{U}\) with elements indexed by \(i=1,\dots,N\)

  • Covariates, \(x_i \in \mathcal{X}\)
  • Treatment variable, \(A_i \in \mathcal{A}\)
  • Potential outcomes, \(\{y_i(a)\}_{a \in \mathcal{A}}\), with \(y_i(a) \in \mathcal{Y}\)

  • \(y_i(A_1, \dots, A_N) = y_i(A_i)\): outcomes for \(i\) depend only on \(i\)’s own treatment — the “stable unit treatment value assumption” (SUTVA), or “no interference”.
  • Unit level causal effects are fixed a priori: compare \(y_i(a)\) to \(y_i(\tilde{a})\). Effects are defined in an “agnostic”, “non-parametric” way.
  • Potential outcomes and covariates are non-random. Treatment is random.

Examples of causal effects

Suppose \(\mathcal{A} = \{0, 1\}\), and define observed outcomes as \(y_i \equiv A_i y_i(1) + (1 - A_i) y_i(0)\).

  • Unit level treatment effect: \(\tau_i = y_i(1) - y_i(0)\)

  • Average treatment effect (ATE): \(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \left(y_i(1) - y_i(0)\right)\)

  • Average effect of treatment on the treated (ATT): \(\frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^N A_i} \sum_{i:A_i=1} \left(y_i(1) - y_i(0)\right)\)

Many more become available once we add mediators or relax SUTVA, e.g.

  • average causal mediation effects
  • average global treatment effect \(\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \left(y_i(\mathbf{1}) - y_i(\mathbf{0})\right)\) under interference (session 12).

Manipulability

  • Effects are defined by letting only treatments vary, holding units fixed. (“Clear counterfactual comparison.”)
  • Thus, causal effects are clearly defined for units that can conceivably receive different treatment values.
    • A test for the above is manipulation:
    • (Holland 1986): “For causal inference, it is critical that each unit be potentially exposable to any one of the causes.”
    • (Angrist and Krueger 1999): “The problem of ambiguous counterfactuals is typically resolved by focusing on hypothetic manipulations in the world as is.”
  • What do we mean by race or gender as causes? (Sen and Wasow 2016)
  • This test may also entail questions of power to change the world (Dimmery and Munger 2025).

What do we mean by ‘identification’?

  • Identification refers generally to sufficiency for drawing a conclusion given the type of data that are available.
  • Ambiguity due to lack of identification is distinct from uncertainty due to sampling.

Studies of identification seek to characterize the conclusions that could be drawn if one could…obtain an unlimited number of observations. Identification problems cannot be solved by gathering more of the same kind of data.

— (Manski 1995, 4)

  • Identification analysis shows how to use assumptions on the data generating process to go from observed outcomes to counterfactual/potential outcomes.
  • Identification strategy is a way to make use of such assumptions to generate causal estimates (Angrist and Krueger 1999).
  • This class mostly focuses not on identification, but on what comes before (experimental design) and what comes after (estimation).

Causal identification with POs

  • Superpopulation setting: the data are a representative random sample from some notional population, \(\mathcal{U}\), countable but large (possibly infinite).
  • Consider a random draw, \(i\), from \(\mathcal{U}\); \(E[\cdot]\) is the expected value for such a draw.
    • Capital letters carry this ex ante uncertainty: a covariate vector \(X_i\), a treatment assignment \(A_i \in \{0,1\}\), and, under SUTVA, potential outcomes \(Y_i(1)\) and \(Y_i(0)\).
  • The unit level effect is \(\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\), so that \(E[\tau_i] = \tau\), the average treatment effect.
  • For an arbitrary draw, we observe \(Y_i = A_i Y_i(1) + (1 - A_i) Y_i(0)\).

Consider the expected difference in means:

\[E[Y_i\mid A_i = 1] - E[Y_i\mid A_i = 0] = E[Y_i(\hlred{1})\mid A_i = 1] - E[Y_i(\hlred{0})\mid A_i = 0]\]

Then what does this difference equal?

Decompositions

Various decompositions are possible. E.g. consider a decomposition wrt the ATT:

\[ \begin{align} E[Y_i\mid A_i = 1] - E[Y_i\mid A_i = 0] &= E[Y_i(1)\mid A_i = 1] - E[Y_i(0)\mid A_i = 0]\\ &= \underbrace{E[Y_i(1)\mid A_i = 1] - \hlblue{E[Y_i(0)\mid A_i = 1]}}_{\text{Average treatment effect on the treated (ATT)}}\\ &+ \underbrace{\hlblue{E[Y_i(0)\mid A_i = 1]} - E[Y_i(0)\mid A_i = 0]}_{\text{Selection bias}}. \end{align} \]

  • Biased for the ATT when \(Y_i(0)\)’s of treated differ from those of controls.
  • Exercise: what is the analogous decomposition with respect to the ATC?

Causal identification under the PO model

Identifying assumption 1 (random assignment):

\[A_i \perp (Y_i(1), Y_i(0)) \quad\text{and}\quad 0 < \Pr[A_i = 1] < 1 \qquad (*)\]

Under \((*)\), the selection bias term vanishes,

\[\underbrace{E[Y_i(0)\mid A_i = 1] - E[Y_i(0)\mid A_i = 0]}_{\text{Selection bias}} = 0,\]

and the ATT is the ATE,

\[\underbrace{E[Y_i(1)\mid A_i = 1] - E[Y_i(0)\mid A_i = 1]}_{\text{ATT}} = E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)] = \tau.\]

Both hold because conditioning on \(A_i\) is uninformative about \((Y_i(1), Y_i(0))\).

So the difference in means identifies the ATE. We now turn to the steps that follow identification — estimation and inference — for a randomized experiment on a random sample.

Population, target, and design

Population

  • A large population \(\mathcal{U}\) of units.
  • We consider a treatment, \(A_j \in \{0, 1\}\), for which each unit \(j \in \mathcal{U}\) has potential outcomes, \((y_j(1), y_j(0))\).
  • Unit level causal effect \(\tau_j = y_j(1) - y_j(0)\).
  • Each unit is also characterized by a continuous covariate, \(x_j\).

Target

  • Population average treatment effect (PATE):

\[\tau := \frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{U}\rvert} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{U}} \left(y_j(1) - y_j(0)\right) = E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)],\]

where \(E[\cdot]\) is with respect to drawing a unit from \(\mathcal{U}\) at random with equal probability.

Design-based uncertainty

Consider the whole population “inference” problem again:

  • A potential outcome is revealed only when the associated treatment is assigned: we observe \(y_j = A_j y_j(1) + (1 - A_j) y_j(0)\).

  • Therefore, we cannot directly compute our target quantity: \[\tau := \frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{U}\rvert} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{U}} \left(y_j(1) - y_j(0)\right)\]

  • The assignment \(A_j\) is equivalent to a sampling indicator, sampling potential outcomes.

  • The treated group in the population is a sample of \(y(1)\) values, and the control group is a sample of \(y(0)\) values.

  • So questions of statistical inference do arise for causal quantities even when you observe every unit in the population.

  • (Abadie et al. 2020): “design-based uncertainty”

From population to sample

  • Now consider a design that includes both sampling and random assignment (two sources of uncertainty).
  • Draw a random sample (e.g., SRSWOR) from \(\mathcal{U}\) and call it \(\mathcal{S}\). Slots in \(\mathcal{S}\) are indexed by \(i = 1, \ldots, N\).
  • An arbitrary member of \(\mathcal{S}\) is characterized by potential outcomes, \((Y_i(1), Y_i(0))\), and a covariate, \(X_i\); with unit level effect \(\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\).
  • Sample average treatment effect (SATE):

\[\tau_{\mathcal{S}} := \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} \left(Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\right) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} \tau_i\]

  • SATE is a random quantity with distribution from the sampling design.
  • For any given \(\mathcal{S}\), SATE may not equal the PATE:
    • sampling-based uncertainty we need to account for.

Complete random assignment

  • We randomly assign \(1 < N_1 < N - 1\) units to treatment \((A_i = 1)\), in which case \(N_0 = N - N_1\) are assigned to control. We observe \(Y_i = A_i Y_i(1) + (1 - A_i) Y_i(0)\).
  • Consider an intuitive estimator for the SATE,

\[\hat{\tau} = \frac{1}{N_1} \sum_{i: A_i=1} Y_i - \frac{1}{N_0} \sum_{i: A_i=0} Y_i = \bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_0.\]

  • For any given treatment assignment, this will not equal SATE exactly: design-based uncertainty. Total uncertainty = sampling-based + design-based.

Let \(E_A[\cdot \mid \mathcal{S}]\) mean “expectations over assignments, holding \(\mathcal{S}\) fixed.” Complete random assignment is SRSWOR of the sample potential outcomes, so

\[E_A[\hat{\tau}\mid \mathcal{S}] = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} \left(Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\right) = \tau_{\mathcal{S}}, \qquad E\big[E_A[\hat{\tau}\mid \mathcal{S}]\big] = \tau.\]

\(\hat{\tau}\) is unbiased for SATE, and — under random sampling too — for PATE.

The randomization variance

Complete random assignment is like SRSWOR for potential outcomes, so

\[\text{Var}_A[\hat{\tau} \mid \mathcal{S}] = \text{Var}_A[\bar{Y}_1 \mid \mathcal{S}] + \text{Var}_A[\bar{Y}_0 \mid \mathcal{S}] - 2\text{Cov}_A[\bar{Y}_1, \bar{Y}_0 \mid \mathcal{S}]\]

\[= \frac{s_{Y(1)}^2}{N_1} \left(\frac{N - N_1}{N}\right) + \frac{s_{Y(0)}^2}{N_0} \left(\frac{N - N_0}{N}\right) - 2 \left(-\frac{s_{Y(1),Y(0)}}{N}\right)\]

\[= \frac{s_{Y(1)}^2}{N_1} + \frac{s_{Y(0)}^2}{N_0} - \underbrace{\frac{s_{Y(1)}^2 + s_{Y(0)}^2 - 2s_{Y(1),Y(0)}}{N}}_{\text{numerator} \;=\; \text{Var}_A[\tau_i \mid \mathcal{S}]} \;=\; \frac{s_{Y(1)}^2}{N_1} + \frac{s_{Y(0)}^2}{N_0} - \frac{s_\tau^2}{N}.\]

(\(s^2_\cdot\) is a sample variance and \(s_{\cdot,\cdot}\) a sample covariance.)

Variance identification

\[\text{Var}_A[\hat{\tau} \mid \mathcal{S}] = \frac{s_{Y(1)}^2}{N_1} + \frac{s_{Y(0)}^2}{N_0} - \frac{s_\tau^2}{N}\]

  • The first two terms are identified, the third is not. (Why?)
  • \(s_\tau^2\) enters with a minus sign, so ignoring it overstates the randomization variance.
  • \(\text{Var}_A[\hat{\tau} \mid \mathcal{S}]\) is therefore largest when \(s_\tau^2 = 0\) — when \(\tau_i\) is constant over \(i\) (a linear shift, \(Y_i(1) = \tau + Y_i(0)\)).
    • Effect heterogeneity works in our favour: it pushes the true randomization variance below what we are able to estimate.
  • The variance goes to zero in \(N_1, N_0\), so the distribution of \(\hat{\tau}\) zeroes in on SATE. We say “\(\hat{\tau}\) is consistent for SATE in \(N_1, N_0\).”

Back to the population

  • Now let’s characterize total uncertainty (sampling+design). Recall \(E[\hat{\tau}] = \text{PATE}\).
  • ANOVA theorem: \(\text{Var}[A] = E[\text{Var}[A \mid B]] + \text{Var}[E[A \mid B]]\). (From the CEF decomposition.)

\[\begin{align} \text{Var}[\hat{\tau}] &= E\big[\text{Var}_A[\hat{\tau}\mid \mathcal{S}]\big] + \text{Var}\big[E_A[\hat{\tau}\mid \mathcal{S}]\big]\\ &= E\left[\frac{s_{Y(1)}^2}{N_1} + \frac{s_{Y(0)}^2}{N_0} - \frac{s_\tau^2}{N}\right] + \text{Var}\left[\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} \tau_i\right]\\ &= \frac{\sigma_{Y(1)}^2}{N_1} + \frac{\sigma_{Y(0)}^2}{N_0} \hlred{- \frac{\sigma_\tau^2}{N} + \frac{\sigma_\tau^2}{N}} \;=\; \frac{\sigma_{Y(1)}^2}{N_1} + \frac{\sigma_{Y(0)}^2}{N_0}. \end{align}\]

  • The unidentified term cancels: the sampling variance of SATE is exactly the piece we could not estimate.
  • So \(\hat{\tau}\) is also consistent for PATE in \(N_1, N_0\).

Inference for SATE or PATE

Conventional sample variances are unbiased for these population variances, so

\[\hat{V} = \frac{s_{Y(1)}^2}{N_1} + \frac{s_{Y(0)}^2}{N_0}\]

is unbiased for \(\text{Var}[\hat{\tau}]\) — different than \(\text{Var}_A[\hat{\tau}\mid \mathcal{S}]\).

  • \(\hat{V}\) is the “Neyman Variance Estimator.” Three interpretations:
    • Conservative approximation of the randomization variance, relative to SATE, for arbitrary effects.
    • Unbiased for that randomization variance when the effect is constant.
    • Unbiased for sampling plus randomization variance, relative to PATE, for arbitrary effects.
  • Equiv. to the “HC2” heteroskedasticity robust estimator (Samii and Aronow 2012) — R’s sandwich or estimatr; very close to Eicker-White.
  • Also approximated by a nonparametric bootstrap of \(N_1\) treatment and \(N_0\) control units (Morgan 2017 Prop. 8).

Simulation Studies

Simulation Studies

Computational studies of the properties of some method

  • Simulate ground truth
  • Analyze the data
  • Compare to ground truth

Use them to check:

  • Your understanding
  • Robustness of software
  • The performance of statistical methods
  • Which method works better
  • How to use the method in your work (e.g. sample sizes / power)

A Useful Guide: (Morris, White, and Crowther 2019)

ADEMP

  1. Aims
  2. Data-generating mechanisms
  3. Estimand
  4. Methods
  5. Performance measures

⇒ Implementation

Aims

What are you trying to do with this study method?

It may:

  • be the only available method for a specific problem
  • perform better than an existing method
  • perform slightly less well but be more reliable
  • be less reliable but faster
  • be more robust under model misspecification

So what does that mean we care about?

  • Whether/when the approach converges?
  • Consistency? (large-sample properties)
  • Small-sample properties?
  • Correct variance formula? (e.g. when derived from theory)
  • Robustness to misspecification?
  • Comparison with other approaches?

Data-generating mechanisms

  • Set out how the data will be created
  • Start with something simple, like \(y_i = 1 + x_i + \varepsilon_i\) where \(\varepsilon_i \sim N(0,1)\)
  • This is where a lot of the magic happens as you use what you know about the method to think about what would be good test-cases.
  • Think about where the randomization comes from!

Some options

  1. Simulate data from a known model (“parametric” simulation)
  2. Resample from a set of data
  3. A combination of (1) and (2)
    • Keep covariates fixed, but simulate the outcome
    • Keep everything observed fixed, but simulate the counterfactuals

Estimand and methods

  • What quantity is the analysis trying to estimate?
    • Estimand: the thing we are trying to estimate
    • Estimator: method for estimating an estimand
    • Estimate: number output by applying estimator

Then, the methods:

  • Set out how each simulated data set will be analysed to give an estimate of the estimand.
  • It’s often good to include a familiar ‘benchmark’ method as a check.

Performance measures

What is a good result?

Let’s call the chosen estimand \(\theta\).

Often, a statistical method outputs an estimate \(\hat{\theta}\), its standard error \(\widehat{s}(\hat{\theta})\) and a confidence interval \([\hat{\theta}_{low}, \hat{\theta}_{high}]\).

Properties of \(\hat{\theta}\):

  • Bias
  • Variance
  • MSE
  • Convergence
  • Compute speed

Properties of \(\widehat{s}(\hat{\theta})\):

  • Average magnitude
  • Bias/MSE relative to theory

Properties of CI:

  • Coverage
  • Power
  • Size

Which to use?

  • Don’t mindlessly report everything!
  • Choice of reported measures should relate back to aims.
  • Trade-offs between performance measures:
    • e.g. some bias might be OK if MSE and coverage are good.
  • In general, need ≥3 performance measures capturing
    • is estimator biased? [Bias]
    • is estimator efficient? [EmpSE; Power]
    • is standard error adequate? [ModSE/EmpSE; Coverage]

Demo

Simulated randomised experiment: the difference in means, Neyman’s \(\hat{V}\):

  • \(\hat{\tau}\) is unbiased for the SATE and the PATE, at every \(N\).
  • The same \(\hat{V}\) is unbiased for the total variance and too large for the design variance.
  • The gap is \(s_\tau^2/N\): unestimable, and negative, so we can only be too cautious.
  • Bigger \(N\) shrinks the variance, not the gap. SATE coverage stays above 95%.

A standard error means nothing until you say which population it refers to.

Summary

What to take away

Design-based causal inference

  • Causal effects are contrasts of potential outcomes; the science is fixed, only assignment is random.
  • Randomization kills the selection-bias term, so the difference in means identifies the ATE.
  • Uncertainty has two sources — sampling and design — and Neyman’s \(\hat{V}\) handles both.

Simulation studies

  • Simulation is how we interrogate a method when theory runs out: we know the truth by construction.
  • Structure the study with ADEMP, and let the aims decide what you report.
  • Report at least bias, efficiency, and adequacy of the standard error.

Next week: estimation with covariates — and where machine learning enters.
